### INFRA as the AI Security Substrate

INFRA is the foundational domain — it governs the compute, network, identity, and pipeline substrate on which all other AI security domains run. Platform engineering teams implementing INFRA controls are, in effect, building the security platform that DATA, MODEL, APP, OPS, and GOV controls depend upon.

**ABB Boundary**:
- **INFRA governs**: GPUs, Kubernetes clusters, MLOps CI/CD pipelines, container registries, secrets vaults, network segmentation, and IaC configurations.
- **DATA governs**: The data layer — what is stored and processed on INFRA compute, access controls for training datasets, de-identification pipelines, and retention.  
- **MODEL governs**: The model artifact layer — what is published to and deployed from the model registry, adversarial testing gates in the MLOps pipeline, and inference API security.
- **Boundary interface**: The `Container Image Registry` and `Secrets Provisioning` interfaces are owned by INFRA and consumed by MODEL and APP. The `Infrastructure Security Telemetry` interface is produced by INFRA and consumed by OPS.

Teams implementing INFRA controls SHOULD also read [GUID-SEC-AI-MODEL-2.9.02](../GUID-SEC-AI-MODEL-2.9.02.md) for model-layer controls that sit above the infrastructure layer.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| ML platform security baseline (IaC, CIS benchmarks) | **Owns** | Consumes | Reviews baseline coverage | Audits |
| Container image golden base builds | **Owns** (builds/maintains) | Specifies ML framework versions | Reviews hardening | Audits |
| Container vulnerability scanning in CI/CD | **Owns** | Remediates in application code/deps | Reviews critical findings | Audits |
| Container runtime security monitoring | **Owns** | N/A | Consumes alerts | Audits |
| Kubernetes RBAC and namespace isolation | **Owns** | Requests required permissions | Reviews access grants | Audits |
| GPU resource quotas and MIG partitioning | **Owns** | Defines per-project GPU requirements | Monitors anomalies | Audits |
| Network segmentation (subnets, NetworkPolicies) | **Owns** | N/A | Reviews topology | Audits |
| Private endpoint configuration | **Owns** | N/A | Reviews configuration | Audits |
| Egress proxy and allowlist management | **Owns** | Submits allowlist requests | Reviews egress control | Audits |
| Secrets vault configuration and rotation policy | **Owns** | Designs workflows to tolerate rotation | Reviews audit logs | Audits |
| Secret scanning in CI/CD and notebooks | **Owns** | Responsible for clean code | Reviews detections | Audits |
| MLOps CI/CD pipeline security gates | **Owns** (infrastructure) | Defines quality gates | Reviews security gates | Audits |
| Infrastructure Security Telemetry to SIEM | **Owns** | N/A | Consumes and correlates | Reviews coverage |

### Technical Controls Requiring Platform Implementation

SHOULD-flagged items require documented justification when not implemented.

**Principle 1 — ML Platform Hardening**:
- ML platform IaC definitions are version-controlled and subject to peer review before deployment; ad-hoc console changes to production ML platform configuration SHALL be prohibited.
- A scheduled CSPM scan SHALL run against ML platform configurations at minimum daily; deviation from baseline SHALL generate an alert within 24 hours.

**Principle 2 — Container Security**:
- Container image builds SHALL extend enterprise base images per [STD-APP-CNT-001](../../../../../standards/application/container/STD-APP-CNT-001-container-deployment.md) and [STD-TEC-EKS-006](../../../../../standards/technology/eks/STD-TEC-EKS-006-security.md). These are normative enterprise standards, not illustrative references.
- Container image scanning SHALL block promotion on critical CVEs; high CVEs SHALL require documented sign-off.
- Runtime security tooling SHALL be deployed on all ML workload nodes.

**Principle 3 — Least Privilege IAM**:
- ML platform IAM role definitions SHALL be managed in version-controlled IaC; manual IAM changes SHALL not be applied directly to production environments.
- Quarterly access reviews SHALL be automated and SHALL generate a report of unused permissions for revocation.

**Principle 4 — GPU Isolation**:
- When shared GPU nodes are used for multi-tenant AI workloads, hardware-level GPU partitioning SHALL be configured to prevent cross-tenant memory access. NVIDIA MIG is the illustrative technology for A100/H100 GPUs; equivalent isolation SHALL be required for other GPU types.
- GPU utilization monitoring SHALL detect cryptocurrency mining anomalies and SHALL alert to SecOps within 15 minutes of detection.

**Principle 5 — Network Segmentation**:
- Kubernetes NetworkPolicies with default-deny egress and ingress SHALL be deployed in all AI workload namespaces.
- Dedicated VPCs for AI workloads SHOULD be implemented; document this decision if a shared VPC is used instead.
- Private endpoints for ML platform APIs SHALL be used in production and PHI-processing environments; no public ML platform endpoints in production.
- All ML workload egress SHALL traverse a proxy or NAT gateway with destination allowlists; egress logs SHALL be ingested into SIEM.

**Principle 6 — Secrets Management**:
- All AI/ML service credentials SHALL be stored in the enterprise secrets management service per [ADR-SEC-002](../../../../../decisions/security/ADR-SEC-002-centralized-secrets-strategy.md). This is a normative enterprise decision record, not an illustrative reference.
- Secret rotation for ML database credentials and service accounts SHALL be automated; rotation cycle SHALL be ≤90 days.
- Pre-commit hooks preventing secret commits to Git SHALL be installed in all ML project repositories.

**Principle 7 — Secure MLOps CI/CD**:
- MLOps pipeline definitions SHALL be stored as code in version-controlled repositories; manual pipeline execution outside of the defined pipeline SHALL require a documented exception.
- Every production ML deployment SHALL have an associated deployment approval record in the audit trail (who approved, when, for which artifact version).

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-RAD-3.9.03.md#pattern-1-iac-managed-ml-platform-security-baseline]

### Pattern 1: IaC-Managed ML Platform Security Baseline

**Purpose**: Ensure consistent, auditable, and drift-resistant ML platform configuration through infrastructure-as-code with automated compliance validation.

**Design**:
- All ML platform resources (Kubernetes clusters, GPU node pools, MLOps platform configurations, IAM roles, network topology) are defined in version-controlled IaC templates.
- IaC templates embed security baselines: private endpoint configurations, encryption settings, IAM policy constraints, logging configurations.
- Every proposed IaC change undergoes peer review and automated policy validation (a policy-as-code gate that validates the plan against security baseline rules) before apply.
- After apply, a cloud security posture management (CSPM) scan runs within 24 hours and generates a report; critical deviations from baseline automatically create an incident ticket.

**Illustrative tooling**: Terraform or CloudFormation for IaC; Checkov, tfsec, or cloud-native policy tools for IaC policy validation; AWS Config, Azure Policy, or third-party CSPM platforms (Prisma Cloud, Wiz) for CSPM scanning.

**NIST SP 800-53**: CM-2 (Baseline Configuration), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), CM-6 (Configuration Settings)

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-RAD-3.9.03.md#pattern-2-hardened-ml-container-lifecycle]

### Pattern 2: Hardened ML Container Lifecycle

**Purpose**: Produce ML containers that meet enterprise security hardening requirements and maintain that security posture throughout the container's lifecycle.

**Design**:
- **Golden base image pipeline**: Enterprise builds and maintains golden base images for common ML frameworks (GPU-enabled PyTorch/TensorFlow images, CPU inference images). These images extend the enterprise hardened OS base, apply non-root user configuration, remove unnecessary OS packages, and set read-only root filesystem where architecturally feasible.
- **Build-time scanning**: Every container image build triggers an automated vulnerability scan. Images with critical CVEs are blocked from the registry; high CVEs require engineering review and approval before promotion.
- **Image signing**: All images that pass scanning are automatically signed with the organizational signing key. The container registry enforces signed-image-only admission.
- **Deployment-time verification**: An admission controller (e.g., OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno) validates image signatures, minimum version requirements, and resource limits before any pod is scheduled on ML nodes.
- **Runtime monitoring**: A runtime security agent deployed on all ML worker nodes detects anomalous container behavior: unexpected process spawning, network destination violations, filesystem write violations, and privilege escalation syscalls.

**Enterprise standards reference**: This pattern SHALL implement [STD-APP-CNT-001](../../../../../standards/application/container/STD-APP-CNT-001-container-deployment.md) and [STD-TEC-EKS-006](../../../../../standards/technology/eks/STD-TEC-EKS-006-security.md) requirements for ML container workloads.

**Illustrative tooling**: Trivy or Grype for vulnerability scanning; Sigstore/Cosign or Notary for image signing; Falco or Tetragon for runtime monitoring; OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno for admission control.

**NIST SP 800-53**: SI-7 (Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity), CM-7 (Least Functionality), SI-4 (Information System Monitoring)

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-RAD-3.9.03.md#pattern-3-kubernetes-ml-workload-isolation]

### Pattern 3: Kubernetes ML Workload Isolation

**Purpose**: Enforce team-level and workload-type isolation for ML compute, preventing cross-team data access and limiting blast radius of compromised workloads.

**Design**:
- **Namespace-per-team architecture**: Each ML team or project receives a dedicated Kubernetes namespace. RBAC roles are scoped to namespaces; team members cannot access other teams' namespaces.
- **Default-deny NetworkPolicies**: Every namespace deploys a default-deny ingress and egress NetworkPolicy at namespace creation. Explicit allow rules are added per approved communication path (e.g., training pods to feature store endpoints, model serving pods to monitoring endpoints).
- **GPU node pool isolation**: GPU nodes are provisioned in a dedicated node pool with appropriate taints. Only pods with the corresponding toleration (enforced via admission controller, not user-configurable) are scheduled on GPU nodes.
- **Resource quotas and limits**: Each namespace has ResourceQuotas defining maximum CPU, memory, and GPU allocations. Each pod has default and maximum LimitRange values applied.
- **Pod Security Standards**: The "restricted" Pod Security Standard is enforced by default across ML namespaces; exceptions for GPU access (which may require specific kernel capabilities) are documented per namespace with a justification record.

**Illustrative tooling**: Native Kubernetes primitives (RBAC, NetworkPolicy, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, Pod Security Admission) are the primary mechanism. Cilium or Calico for advanced NetworkPolicy enforcement.

**NIST SP 800-53**: AC-6 (Least Privilege), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), SC-7 (Boundary Protection), SC-6 (Resource Availability)

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-RAD-3.9.03.md#pattern-4-gpu-security-and-crypto-mining-detection]

### Pattern 4: GPU Security and Crypto-Mining Detection

**Purpose**: Enforce hardware-level isolation between GPU workloads and detect unauthorized GPU usage (cryptocurrency mining or resource abuse).

**Design**:
- **Hardware partitioning**: On multi-tenant GPU nodes, hardware-level partitioning is configured at the GPU hardware level. This prevents cross-tenant GPU memory access even under resource pressure. Partition assignments are managed by the infrastructure team and scoped per project. NVIDIA MIG is the illustrative mechanism for A100/H100 GPUs; equivalent isolation mechanisms SHALL be applied for other GPU types.
- **Usage monitoring**: Per-pod GPU utilization, memory consumption, and compute process names are collected from the GPU management layer (NVIDIA DCGM is the illustrative stack; similar data is available from other GPU vendors).
- **Anomaly detection**: Automated rules detect cryptocurrency mining indicators: sustained ≥95% GPU utilization outside of scheduled training jobs, process names matching known mining executables, and anomalous outbound network connections from GPU pods to known mining pool IP ranges.
- **Cost governance**: GPU usage is tagged per team and project. Unexpected cost spikes (>2× historical baseline) generate an alert and trigger a review workflow before the spike can continue unabated.

**Illustrative tooling**: NVIDIA DCGM for GPU telemetry; Prometheus with custom alert rules for anomaly detection; cloud cost management tools for cost anomaly detection.

**NIST SP 800-53**: SC-6 (Resource Availability), AU-2 (Audit Events), SI-4 (Information System Monitoring)

---
page_texts.14:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-RAD-3.9.03.md#pattern-5-ml-network-segmentation-and-egress-control]

### Pattern 5: ML Network Segmentation and Egress Control

**Purpose**: Limit lateral movement from compromised ML workloads, prevent data exfiltration, and control access to external resources from within the ML compute environment.

**Design**:
- **VPC topology** (illustrative): ML workloads are deployed in dedicated subnets organized by workload type:
  - Training subnets: Private, no internet gateway, NAT gateway with proxy for approved egress only
  - Inference subnets: Private, inbound traffic only from application VPCs via dedicated connectivity (PrivateLink or VPC peering), egress through proxy
  - Experimentation subnets: Isolated, restricted access to production data stores, limited approved egress
- **Private endpoints**: ML platform APIs (managed training services, model registries, data stores) are accessed via private endpoints from within the ML VPC. No public IP-based access to ML platform APIs is permitted in production.
- **Egress proxy**: All outbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic from ML workloads routes through a forward proxy with a maintained allowlist including: approved package repositories, cloud provider APIs, organizational source control, and approved external model repositories. Attempted connections to destinations outside the allowlist are blocked and logged.
- **DLP at egress**: The egress proxy inspects outbound content for PHI and credential patterns. Matches generate security alerts; sensitive-data matches may be blocked depending on policy.

**Illustrative tooling**: AWS VPC / Azure VNet for network topology; Squid or cloud-native proxy (AWS Network Firewall, Azure Firewall) for egress control; cloud PrivateLink for private endpoint connectivity.

**NIST SP 800-53**: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), SC-5 (Denial-of-Service Protection), AC-17 (Remote Access)

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-RAD-3.9.03.md#pattern-6-secrets-management-for-ml-workflows]

### Pattern 6: Secrets Management for ML Workflows

**Purpose**: Eliminate hardcoded credentials from ML code and notebooks; enforce centralized secrets storage, dynamic injection, and automated rotation for all AI/ML service credentials.

**Enterprise decision reference**: This pattern implements [ADR-SEC-002 — Centralized Secrets Strategy](../../../../../decisions/security/ADR-SEC-002-centralized-secrets-strategy.md) requirements for AI/ML workloads. Teams SHALL comply with ADR-SEC-002 for all ML secret management decisions.

**Design**:
- **Centralized vault**: All ML credentials (database passwords, API keys for external services, cloud credentials for service accounts, model signing keys) are stored in the enterprise-approved secrets management service.
- **Dynamic injection**: Secrets are injected into ML workloads at runtime via secrets manager integration (e.g., Kubernetes Secrets Store CSI driver mounting secrets as volumes, or managed ML platform's built-in secrets injection for training jobs). Secrets are NEVER stored in container images, IaC templates, notebooks, or source code.
- **Automated rotation**: Rotation is configured to execute automatically within the vault for supported credential types (database passwords, API keys). ML workflows are designed to fetch credentials fresh on each invocation, tolerating rotation transparently.
- **Secret scanning prevention**: Pre-commit hooks (e.g., git-secrets, gitleaks, or TruffleHog) are required in all ML project repositories and prevent commits containing credential patterns. CI/CD pipelines also scan for secrets in pushed code.
- **Notebook scanning**: Jupyter notebooks submitted to version control pass through a secrets scanner before merge; notebooks with credentials are rejected.

**Illustrative tooling**: AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, or HashiCorp Vault for storage; Secrets Store CSI Driver for Kubernetes injection; git-secrets, gitleaks, or TruffleHog for pre-commit scanning.

**NIST SP 800-53**: IA-5 (Authenticator Management), SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), AU-2 (Audit Events)

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-RAD-3.9.03.md#pattern-7-secure-mlops-cicd-pipeline]

### Pattern 7: Secure MLOps CI/CD Pipeline

**Purpose**: Prevent supply chain attacks, unauthorized deployments, and unreviewed changes from reaching the ML compute environment via the MLOps pipeline.

**Design**:
- **Security gates in pipeline**: The MLOps CI/CD pipeline includes mandatory, non-bypassable automated security gates:
  1. Container vulnerability scan (blocks on critical CVEs)
  2. ML dependency scan (Python packages, requirements files)
  3. Secret scan (rejects pipeline run if secrets detected in code)
  4. IaC policy validation (validates infrastructure changes against security baseline)
  5. Artifact signing (container images, model artifacts signed before registry upload)
  6. Production deployment approval gate (requires human approval record)
- **Pipeline definition immutability**: Pipeline definitions are stored as code in version-controlled repositories. Changes to pipeline definitions require peer review and merge approval. Manual pipeline execution with modified definitions is blocked.
- **Deployment audit trail**: Every pipeline execution writes a structured audit record including: pipeline ID, trigger identity (user or automation), artifact versions deployed, gates passed/failed, approver identity (for production deployments), and timestamp. Deployment audit records are forwarded to the enterprise SIEM.

**Illustrative tooling**: Tekton, Argo Workflows, Kubeflow Pipelines, or cloud-native CI/CD platforms for pipeline execution; Trivy or Grype for container scanning; pip-audit/Safety for Python dependency scanning; OPA or Checkov for IaC policy validation.

**NIST SP 800-53**: SA-10 (Developer Configuration Management), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), AU-2 (Audit Events), NIST SSDF PO.3

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-RAD-3.9.03.md#training-infrastructure]

### Training Infrastructure

**Lifecycle stage**: Provisioning → Active training → Post-training cleanup

| Phase | Key Controls | NIST SP 800-53 |
|---|---|---|
| Provisioning | IaC deployment with security baseline; network isolation configured; IAM role attached | CM-2, AC-3, SC-7 |
| Active training | No internet access; all data access logged; GPU partitioning active; audit logging enabled | AU-2, SC-7, SC-6 |
| Post-training | Ephemeral compute terminated; training data connections revoked; artifacts published to registry | CM-8, MP-6 |
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-RAD-3.9.03.md#inference-infrastructure]

### Inference Infrastructure

**Lifecycle stage**: Initial deployment → Serving → Upgrade → Decommission

| Phase | Key Controls | NIST SP 800-53 |
|---|---|---|
| Initial deployment | Signed image verified; model artifact hash verified; private endpoint configured; rate limiter configured | SI-7, SC-7, AC-3 |
| Serving | Runtime monitoring active; telemetry to SIEM; periodic integrity re-verification; auto-scaling within approved limits | SI-4, AU-2, SC-6 |
| Upgrade | Blue/green or canary pattern; new image passes all pipeline gates; rollback target confirmed | CM-3, SI-7 |
| Decommission | Endpoints disabled; credentials revoked from vault; network policies cleaned up | AC-2, IA-5 |
